Massachusetts.right_to_work_note: Massachusetts has no right-to-work law, so a union contract can require workers in a union job to pay dues or fees.
Massachusetts.public_bargaining_note: Most state, county, and city workers can form a union and bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions under Chapter 150E.
Massachusetts.public_strike_note: Massachusetts law bars public employees from striking, so contract disputes go to mediation, fact-finding, or arbitration instead.
Massachusetts.state_note: In 2023 lawmakers filed a bill to let some public workers strike after long contract talks, but it did not pass, so the strike ban still stands.

Michigan.right_to_work_note: Michigan repealed its right-to-work law in 2023, and the repeal took effect in March 2024, so union contracts can again require dues or fees.
Michigan.public_bargaining_note: Michigan public workers can unionize and bargain under the Public Employment Relations Act, which requires employers to bargain in good faith.
Michigan.public_strike_note: Michigan law says a public employee shall not strike, and courts can order striking workers back to work.
Michigan.state_note: Michigan was the first state in nearly 60 years to repeal a right-to-work law, but public workers still cannot be forced to pay union fees because of a Supreme Court decision called Janus.

Minnesota.right_to_work_note: Minnesota has no right-to-work law, so union contracts can require workers to pay dues or fees.
Minnesota.public_bargaining_note: Minnesota public workers can unionize and bargain under the Public Employment Labor Relations Act, which covers state, county, city, and school workers.
Minnesota.public_strike_note: Public workers who are not essential can strike after their contract ends and mediation steps are done, but essential workers such as police and prison guards cannot strike.
Minnesota.state_note: Minnesota is one of the few states where some public workers can legally strike, but only workers who are not essential and only after mediation steps are finished.

Mississippi.right_to_work_note: Mississippi's constitution and state law say no worker can be required to join a union or pay union dues to keep a job.
Mississippi.public_bargaining_note: Mississippi has no law giving public workers the right to bargain, so state and local workers cannot negotiate a binding union contract.
Mississippi.public_strike_note: Public workers in Mississippi are barred from striking.
Mississippi.state_note: Mississippi is one of the few states with no public-sector bargaining law at all, and it has no state labor-relations board, so private-sector union complaints go to the federal labor board.

Missouri.right_to_work_note: Missouri voters rejected a right-to-work law in 2018, so union contracts can still require dues or fees.
Missouri.public_bargaining_note: Missouri's constitution gives public workers the right to bargain, but the employer can reject parts of a deal and there is no binding arbitration.
Missouri.public_strike_note: Missouri law gives public workers no right to strike, and union contracts must say that striking can mean immediate firing.
Missouri.state_note: Missouri voters rejected right-to-work by about two to one in August 2018, before the law ever took effect.

Montana.right_to_work_note: Montana has no right-to-work law, so union contracts can require workers to pay dues or fees.
Montana.public_bargaining_note: Montana public workers can form unions and bargain over pay, hours, and working conditions under the Public Employees Collective Bargaining Act.
Montana.public_strike_note: Montana courts have read the bargaining law to allow public-worker strikes because no statute bans them, but police officers are barred from striking and use binding arbitration instead.
Montana.state_note: Montana is unusual because its Supreme Court ruled in 1974 that public workers may strike, since the law protects concerted activities and bans strikes only for police.

Nebraska.right_to_work_note: Nebraska's constitution bans requiring workers to join a union or pay dues to keep a job.
Nebraska.public_bargaining_note: Nebraska public workers can form unions and bargain under the State Employees Collective Bargaining Act and the Industrial Relations Act.
Nebraska.public_strike_note: Nebraska law says no one may stop government services by striking, and public workers have no right to strike.
Nebraska.state_note: Nebraska settles public-sector pay disputes through its Commission of Industrial Relations, which can set wages instead of letting workers strike.

Nevada.right_to_work_note: Nevada law bars contracts that require workers to join a union or pay dues to keep a job.
Nevada.public_bargaining_note: Nevada local government workers have long had bargaining rights, and a 2019 law extended them to state workers.
Nevada.public_strike_note: Nevada law declares strikes by state and local government workers illegal.
Nevada.state_note: Nevada gave state workers the right to bargain only in 2019, and in 2023 a court ruled a coordinated teacher sick-out an illegal strike.

New Hampshire.right_to_work_note: New Hampshire has no right-to-work law, and the latest attempt to pass one was killed by the House in February 2025.
New Hampshire.public_bargaining_note: New Hampshire public workers can organize and bargain under RSA 273-A, which covers state, county, city, school, and university workers.
New Hampshire.public_strike_note: New Hampshire law says strikes and other job actions by public workers are unlawful.
New Hampshire.agency_name: New Hampshire Public Employee Labor Relations Board
New Hampshire.state_note: New Hampshire lawmakers have voted down right-to-work bills repeatedly, most recently in February 2025, even though the governor at the time favored one.

New Jersey.right_to_work_note: New Jersey has no right-to-work law, so union contracts can require workers to pay dues or fees.
New Jersey.public_bargaining_note: New Jersey public workers can bargain under the Employer-Employee Relations Act, with the Public Employment Relations Commission handling disputes.
New Jersey.public_strike_note: New Jersey has no statute giving public workers a right to strike, and its courts have ruled walkouts unlawful and can order workers back.
New Jersey.agency_name: New Jersey Public Employment Relations Commission
New Jersey.state_note: New Jersey's constitution gives public workers the right to organize and present grievances, but it does not grant a right to strike, so courts treat public-worker strikes as unlawful.
